After: D and both of its edges are gone, shown as dashed outlines, leaving the path C, A, B." width="100%"} Removes a node and all its incident edges from the graph. The node can be specified by its ID or label. Every edge that starts or ends at the node is removed too (including self-loops and parallel edges), since an edge can't exist without both endpoints. The remaining nodes keep their IDs, and the deleted ID is not reused for nodes added later. The graph is modified in place, and the deletion is recorded in the step log (see `steps`). If the node was selected, it is also dropped from the node selection, and its removed edges are dropped from the edge selection. Use it to prune individual nodes, e.g., removing an outlier, an isolated node or a known hub before re-running an analysis. To delete many nodes at once based on a condition, select them and call `delete_nodes_ws()` instead. Note that removing a node can split the graph into several components. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to delete, given as an integer node ID or a string label. If a label is used and several nodes share it, only the node that the label resolves to is removed. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Returns self to enable method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NodeNotFoundError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the node doesn't exist in the graph (either an unknown label or an unknown ID). It is a subclass of `KeyError` (which this method has always raised) and of `ValueError`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Deleting a node also removes every edge incident to it. Here, "B" is the middle of a three-node path with two edges: ::: {#3e65b500 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, 2) ``` ::: ::: After deleting "B", both of its edges are gone, leaving "A" and "C" disconnected: ::: {#cd7d06ac .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.delete_node(node="B") graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges(), graph.has_node(node="B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (2, 0, False) ``` ::: ::: Nodes can also be deleted by internal ID rather than label: ::: {#79462bea .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_node(label="Alice") node_id = graph.get_id_from_label(label="Alice") graph.delete_node(node=node_id) graph.has_node(node=node_id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Deleting a node that doesn't exist raises a `KeyError`: ::: {#e7867e08 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: graph.delete_node(node="Zed") except KeyError as e: print(e) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Node with label 'Zed' not found in graph ``` ::: :::
